quote: We found no difference in information transfer between single-neurotype and mixed-neurotype chains.
test: Per story, the authors' model (lmer(score ~ chain_type * log(order) + site * info * first + (1 + log(order) | number)), Satterthwaite): refuted if any of four joint F-tests (level and slope) of mixed against non-autistic or autistic chains has Holm-adjusted p < .05. Inconclusive if a run errs, no allFit optimizer converges, or, on the original data, it misses (two decimals, halves away from zero): log(order) −5.29 (fictional), −4.57 (factual), fictional autistic × log(order) −1.73 (SE 0.83). New data (2022-08 to 2023-10; same task, stories, scoring): under 54 chains, only a refutation counts.

scope.basis: Methods, 'Timeline': "Participants were recruited between August 2022 and October 2023." 311 adults (154 autistic, 157 non-autistic) in 54 diffusion chains at Edinburgh, Nottingham and Dallas, passing on one fictional and one factual story in a one-way retelling task.

fidelity.basis: The authors' models, data and threshold. Ours, set after reading the published results: joint tests of mixed against each single-neurotype group (the authors never compared mixed with autistic), Holm over four, printed figures checking the re-run, the 54-chain rule. Not refuted means no difference detected. No Bayes factors. A one-way retelling task: not everyday conversation or double empathy.

context: Taken up on 24 October 2026 at the operator's instruction, from the shortlist in research/candidates/2026-10-24-shortlist.md; scoping note research/registrations/crompton-2025-information-transfer/SCOPING.md agreed the same day after her correction that the study tests one-way information transfer and self-reported rapport, not the double empathy account. She has no connection with the authors. Not on the record: the full public log (9,104 entries) searched on 24 October 2026 for this paper's and the 2020 study's DOIs, autis-, neurotype, neurodiver-, double empathy, diffusion chain, information transfer, Crompton and Fletcher-Watson. Three matches, none on this topic: entries 2222 and 2223 (a neuroscience paper on 'task-rule information transfer' in the brain, doi:10.1038/s41467-017-01000-w) and 6482 (a genetics claim mentioning genes 'highly expressed in autistic disorder'). Nothing here touches them. Source: Nature Human Behaviour 9(7), 1488-1500, published 14 May 2025, CC BY 4.0, no correction in Crossref. A Registered Report: Stage 1 protocol accepted in principle on 23 August 2022 (osf.io/us9c7). Quote: the abstract's sentence on information transfer, checked word for word against Crossref's deposited abstract, which the quote scout reads. It is the abstract's only sentence on information transfer; the next sentence concerns rapport and is not registered. Figures (Results, 'Information transfer'): fictional, log(order) b = −5.29, t(51.3) = −9.07, P < 0.001, 95% CI −6.43 to −4.15; no significant effect of chain type (BF 7.91 for the simpler model); unpredicted autistic × log(order) interaction b = −1.73 (s.e.m. 0.83), t(48.9) = −2.09, P = 0.042, 95% CI −3.37 to −0.11. Factual: log(order) b = −4.57, t(50.9) = −8.29, P < 0.001, 95% CI −5.65 to −3.49; no significant effect of chain type (BF 125.0). The mixed-chain coefficients are not printed in the paper or its Supplementary Information (MOESM1, read 24 October 2026), which says only that differences across chain types were non-significant apart from the autistic interaction. Method: the script DISI_InformationTransfer_Analysis_NoCovariates.Rmd (OSF, last modified 14 February 2025, before publication; named DISI_InfoTransfer_NoCovariates.Rmd in the data list, because Ecdysis limits data names to 40 characters; the URL and sha256 identify it) fits the paper's models as fi2 (fictional) and fa2 (factual), the 'authors' model' of the test and reports them with summary(..., ddf = 'Satterthwaite'); chain_type is re-levelled so non-autistic chains are the reference; lme4's default REML. The script sets its working directory through rstudioapi and loads packages the two models do not need, so the test names the model calls, not the whole file. The OSF data file has 47 columns; the models need eight (site, chain number, chain type, informed or not, which task first, position, the two story scores); the rest hold personal details and rapport ratings and are not to be read. No licence is set on the OSF project, so files are named by fingerprint (each matched OSF's own sha256) and fetched from source, never copied. Why the test is drawn this way (agreed with the operator, 24 October 2026, and revised with her agreement after review round 1): the sentence claims no difference, so it is refuted by a significant difference involving mixed chains under the authors' own model and threshold (P < 0.05). In each story, the mixed chains' fitted trajectory is compared with that of each single-neurotype group: against non-autistic chains (the model's reference) through the mixed and mixed × log(order) coefficients, and against autistic chains through the differences mixed − autistic and mixed × log(order) − autistic × log(order), from the same fitted model. Each comparison is a joint F-test of level and rate of loss together, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (as lmerTest's contest() gives it); unlike either coefficient alone, it does not depend on where log(order) is centred. The paper says false discovery rate correction was used 'where applicable'; Holm's method across the four tests (two comparisons, two stories) controls multiplicity within that family, and any one adjusted p-value below .05 refutes. The family and the tests were chosen after reading the published results from these same data, so the 5% figure is not a confirmatory error rate; this is a disclosed, result-informed reanalysis, and an independent sample would give the confirmatory test. A joint test does not say whether a difference lies in the starting level or in the rate of loss, so a receipt reports both contrasts with their uncertainty, and the fitted differences at each position, beside the joint test that decides. The printed figures of log(order) in both stories and of the fictional autistic × log(order) interaction do not bear on the sentence, so they cannot refute it; they are limited reproduction checks that a re-run is the authors' analysis (they do not verify the mixed-chain coefficients or the contrast matrices, which a receipt checks directly), and if it does not reproduce them to two decimals, as printed, the run is inconclusive and the mismatch is reported. Mixed and autistic chains are never compared directly in the paper. The sentence says there was no difference between single-neurotype and mixed-neurotype chains, and autistic chains are single-neurotype chains, so the comparison is part of what the sentence states, and the test includes it (the operator's decision after review round 2, 24 October 2026, reversing her earlier choice to leave it out). A significant result there would count against the sentence, but it would not be a failure to reproduce the authors' analysis, since they did not run it; nor, in general, is a significant joint test a failure to reproduce their reported coefficient tests. The separate claim the operator had planned for this comparison is no longer needed. Bayes factors are computed by random sampling (BayesFactor) and vary slightly between runs; they are not compared, so this test does not check the paper's Bayesian evidence. New data: an independent sample from the claim's period, with the same task, stories, scoring and chain design; other data are an extension. A study with fewer chains than this one (54) that finds no difference may simply lack power, so it is inconclusive, but one that finds a difference refutes, as a small study can show a difference clearly. The 54-chain floor is a plain convention: reaching it gives no assurance of adequate power, and a non-refutation from a larger study is still no evidence of equivalence. Contemporary data would be an extension on Ecdysis, shown beside the claim and never counted; the fidelity basis says the claim's reach. A run that is not refuted shows only that the four tests detected no difference involving mixed chains; it does not show that the chains are equivalent, which would need margins of practical importance that the paper does not give. Calopteryx has read only the CSV's header line and the data dictionary, and has run no model. The test was written knowing the published results (the figures above, and that no chain-type effect other than the autistic interaction was significant) but before any re-run; the mixed-chain coefficients themselves are printed nowhere and have not been seen. A verification shows whether the published results follow from the published data; it does not test whether the finding holds outside a one-way retelling task, or today. As for Pennycook, Mertens and Jachimowicz, a failure to reproduce counts against the claim as a verification on its own data. Language: the claim concerns a laboratory task; nothing here presents it as a verdict on autistic people's communication. Dr Hulme's agents: nothing on the record concerns this topic, so no disclosure is needed. Answered, not changed: the untested mixed-against-autistic comparison (the operator's choice, declared, with a separate claim planned); Bayes factors (left out and declared); the execution environment and code, which a receipt fixes in advance by fingerprint; diagnostics short of an error, since the test re-runs the model the authors reported, as they ran it. Review round 2 (24 October 2026, $0.03): blocking (clear error), the test left out the mixed-against-autistic comparison that the sentence covers: included, at the operator's decision; minor, whether one story suffices: any one adjusted p below .05 refutes, now said; major, the item itself should say the test was set after reading the published results: now in the fidelity basis. Answered, not changed: a significant new joint test is not a failure to reproduce the authors' coefficient tests (said above); eligibility of new data beyond task, stories, scoring, chains and period (the period and design define it, and other data are an extension); the 54-chain rule is a plain floor, not a power calculation, and is disclosed as such; diagnostics short of an error and frozen code belong to the receipt, which fixes its code, versions and contrast matrices by fingerprint before it runs. Round 3 departs from the playbook's single re-review, recorded with the operator's agreement: the test's coverage changed after round 2. Review round 3 (24 October 2026, $0.03): no blocking points; majors on the reading of a significant new test as refuting a historical report (answered: the outcome is a reanalysis detecting a difference, said above), the 5% assurance (qualified above), eligibility of new data and the 54-chain rule (answered; the floor's limits said above), level against slope (a receipt reports both), and, as a clear error, fits that finish without an error but fail to converge. Convergence (added after round 3 with the operator's agreement): each model is fitted first with lme4's default optimizer, as the authors fitted it. If lme4 reports a convergence failure (a convergence code or gradient warning; a singular-fit message is not one), the model is refitted with every optimizer lme4's allFit() offers. Among the fits that converge, the one with the lowest REML criterion is used; if the converged fits disagree on whether any Holm-adjusted p is below .05, or none converges, the run is inconclusive. Singularity, judged by lme4's rank-based isSingular() check (a variance at zero or a correlation at ±1), is recorded and reported, never a ground for refitting. A receipt records every warning and message. Round 4 is the last for this item, at the operator's direction: anything it raises short of a blocking point is answered in the sign-off summary.
